lesson.title: Reading the Map: How to Use a Standard Normal Table
lesson.summary: A standard normal table lists the cumulative probability, the area to the left, for a wide range of z-scores, letting you look up exact probabilities for the standard normal curve rather than relying on the whole-number estimates of the empirical rule.
lesson.body:
A standard normal table, often called a z-table, is a grid of probabilities built for the one standard normal curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Each entry in the table gives the cumulative probability associated with a specific z-score, meaning the proportion of the standard normal distribution lying at or below that z-score, which is the area under the curve to the left of that point. Because every normal distribution can be converted into z-scores through standardization, this one table serves every possible normal distribution, not just one particular mean and standard deviation.

Reading the table is a two-step lookup. Down the left-hand column, z-scores are listed to one decimal place, such as 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, and so on. Across the top row, a second decimal digit is listed, from 0.00 to 0.09. To look up a specific z-score like 1.35, find the row for 1.3 and the column for 0.05, since 1.3 plus 0.05 equals 1.35, and read the value where that row and column intersect. In a standard normal table, that entry is 0.9115.

That value, 0.9115, means that 91.15 percent of the standard normal distribution lies at or below a z-score of 1.35; equivalently, the area under the standard normal curve to the left of z equals 1.35 is 0.9115. Because the total area under any probability curve equals 1, the area to the right of z equals 1.35, meaning the proportion above that z-score, is found by subtraction: 1 minus 0.9115, which equals 0.0885, or 8.85 percent.

The table's numbers also respect the symmetry of the normal curve. Since the curve is a mirror image around z equals 0, the area to the left of a negative z-score equals the area to the right of the corresponding positive z-score. So the area to the left of z equals negative 1.35 is the same 0.0885 found above for the area to the right of positive 1.35, a shortcut that avoids needing a separate table for negative values, since most printed tables include negative z-scores directly, but the symmetry relationship is worth knowing as a check on your work regardless.

The same lookup process works for any z-score in the table's range. For instance, z equals 1.50 gives a cumulative probability of 0.9332, and z equals negative 1.00 gives 0.1587. Practicing several lookups like these, both positive and negative, builds the comfort needed to move quickly between a z-score and its associated area, which is the exact skill required once real, concrete measurements enter the picture rather than abstract z-scores alone.

On its own, a table of z-scores and cumulative probabilities feels abstract, since it is built for a distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 that no real variable actually follows. Its value only becomes clear once it is paired with standardization: convert a real value from any normal distribution into a z-score first, then look that z-score up in this table to get an exact probability. That two-step process, standardize then look up, is exactly the skill developed next in finding normal probabilities for real, concrete situations.
